elements.text: In-flight failure and separation of the right wing during normal flight
Failure of Chalk's Ocean Airways maintenance program to identify and properly repair fatigue cracks in the right wing
Failure of the Federal Aviation Administration to detect and correct deficiencies in the company’s maintenance program
Captain and first officer were properly certificated and qualified
No evidence of medical or behavioral conditions affecting crew performance
No evidence of flight crew fatigue
Accident airplane was certificated and equipped in accordance with Federal regulations
Recovered components showed no evidence of system or powerplant failures
Fire damage to fuselage and empennage resulted from right wing failure and fuel tank breach
Accident was not survivable
Emergency response was timely
No warning provided to flight crew of right wing's imminent failure
Nothing crew could have done to regain control after wing separation
Right wing separated due to preexisting fatigue fractures and cracks in rear Z-stringer, lower skin, and rear spar lower spar cap
Multiple-element fatigue damage reduced residual strength capability of wing structure
Repetitive fuel leaks were indicators of structural damage inside the right wing
Chalk's Ocean Airways likely performed doubler repair to lower skin at wing station 34
Doubler repair was ineffective because it did not restore load-carrying capability in area of fuel sump drain
Repair did not properly address underlying cause of skin cracking (cracked/fractured rear Z-stringer)
Establishment of repair thresholds in maintenance programs would help ensure evaluation of repeated discrepancies
Chalk's Ocean Airways should have performed comprehensive inspection and maintenance on wing structures based on repetitive fuel leaks and prior findings
Chalk's Ocean Airways maintenance program and practices were deficient
Deficiencies in maintenance program and practices were causal to the accident
Chalk's Ocean Airways maintenance program plan was inadequate to maintain structural integrity of aircraft fleet
FAA procedures for maintenance program oversight are insufficient for operators with limited manufacturer support
FAA's failure to identify inadequacy of Chalk's Ocean Airways maintenance program was causal to the accident
Updating FAA Order 8300.10 with CASS guidance would help inspectors ensure effective implementation
FAA received sufficient cues to alert it to potential safety deficiencies at Chalk's Ocean Airways
FAA missed opportunity to recertify Grumman Mallard with new type certificate including fatigue analysis
Fatigue analysis likely would have determined safe operating life for wing structure, preventing accident
